attribution.note: Marcus wrote this third-person line in his own post. It is his own claim about his track record.

semantics.note: Keeps his exact wording, including the 'from day 1' scope. It is a retrospective claim about what he has said.

contract.note: Reading 'day 1' as the start of his LLM commentary is ordinary and fair. Because that start point is not identified, the result depends on how 'day 1' is read.

evidence.note: Independent report that he mocked GPT-2's lack of common sense in October 2019. It shows early skepticism but does not show that this was where his LLM commentary began.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows Marcus criticising GPT-2 in October 2019, which fits a long record of skepticism. Nothing establishes when his LLM commentary began, or that his criticism started at that point. No contradicting early phase appears either. The from-the-outset part is therefore unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps both parts as he wrote them: a meltdown, and that it was unexplained.

contract.note: Judging 'unexplained' as of when he published (Feb 22) is the ordinary reading. Another fair reading, unexplained when it began, would change the result, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: Same-day report of nonsensical ChatGPT output on Feb 21. Supports the meltdown part.

OpenAI's incident page shows a causal explanation (an optimization bug, faulty inference kernels) dated Feb 21, before the post. This is a company disclosure, used here only to show an explanation was public, not that it was true.

reviews.rationale: The meltdown part holds: reporting shows ChatGPT gave incoherent answers on Feb 20–21. The 'unexplained' part fails under the contract: OpenAI published a causal explanation on Feb 21, a day before the Feb 22 post. The contract says this case is mixed.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Uses his exact words. It is a rhetorical complaint about an observed Gemini failure.

contract.note: Reading it as a complaint about a documented error, here the image controversy that week, is a fair ordinary reading. A literal claim of universal inability, or a text-only reading, could change the result.

evidence.note: WIRED, published Feb 22, reports Gemini producing a historically wrong Apollo 11 crew image during the controversy. It is an image failure, not a text one.

reviews.rationale: A reputable report from the same time documents Gemini depicting the Apollo 11 crew incorrectly in February 2024, which meets the contract's support condition. Nothing shows the error was fabricated. A text-identification failure is not shown, and the contract does not require one.
